bp: A retrieval-augmented language model is a question-answering system that does not rely only on what was stored inside the model during training. When a user asks something, the system first searches an outside collection, such as web pages or a knowledge base, then feeds selected documents into the language model so it can build an answer from fresher or more specific evidence. That extra search-and-read pipeline makes the answer more useful, but it also makes each answer more expensive. The system may retrieve documents, read long passages, reason over them, and produce a long response. This paper studies a security problem where the attacker is not trying to make the answer false. The attacker is trying to make the answer costly. The ordinary-world target is a service provider paying for every generated word-like piece of text and every step of model processing. A poisoned outside corpus can silently turn normal user questions into unusually expensive calls.
wh: The hard part is that the attack must pass through the same doorway as helpful information. A retrieval system is supposed to find documents that look relevant to the user's question. If an attacker places documents in the outside corpus, those documents have to look useful enough to be retrieved, but they also have to push the language model toward consuming many more text pieces during inference, which is the run-time answering phase. Earlier inference cost attacks often assume the attacker can directly edit or control the prompt, meaning the exact instruction sent to the model. The paper argues that this is often unrealistic because many users and services keep prompts controlled. Poisoning the external knowledge base is more plausible: the web or another corpus may contain attacker-written documents. The tension is therefore dual. The malicious document must be close enough to the question to be selected, while also shaped to exhaust computation without visibly corrupting answer quality.
naive: A smart beginner might try to paste very long malicious pages into the knowledge base and hope the retrieval system pulls them in. That fails for two reasons. First, irrelevant length is easy for the retriever to ignore, because the page may not match the user's information need. Second, a crude document may damage the final answer, making the attack obvious or filtered out. Another beginner strategy would be to manipulate the user's prompt directly, adding instructions that force a long answer. The abstract says that assumption is impractical in many RAG settings. The attacker needs a subtler route: documents that look semantically relevant, meaning relevant in subject matter and wording, while also inducing abnormal token consumption when the model reads and synthesizes them.
ap: The central move is to treat attack writing as a search problem over documents. The paper introduces RA-ICA, a retrieval-augmented inference cost attack, where the attacker injects malicious documents into the external corpus rather than touching the user's prompt. It then proposes CREEP, which uses language-model agents as automated writers. These agents try to produce documents that satisfy two pressures at once: they should be likely to be retrieved for target questions, and they should make the downstream model spend more text budget during answer generation. The paper further tunes those agents with MA-GRPO, a reinforcement learning method, meaning a trial-and-feedback process where generated documents are rewarded when they make the attack stronger. The memory part keeps historical best adversarial documents so new attempts can learn from earlier successful patterns instead of starting fresh every time.
mech: The mechanism begins with an external knowledge corpus, the collection a RAG system searches before answering. The attacker adds crafted documents to that corpus. A normal user then asks a question. The retriever scores documents for relevance and selects some passages. The attack succeeds only if the injected document is among those selected, so CREEP first has to make the malicious document read like a plausible source for the question. After retrieval, the language model receives the selected material and synthesizes an answer. At this point the malicious document is supposed to change the cost shape of inference: it should make the model consume many more tokens, which are the small text units the system processes and bills for, while not obviously breaking the final answer. CREEP uses language-model agents to draft candidate documents. Each candidate can be judged by whether it is retrieved and how much extra generation cost it causes. MA-GRPO then fine-tunes the agents by comparing groups of candidate documents, giving more weight to those that performed better relative to the group. Its memory stores historically strong adversarial documents, so the next round can reuse patterns that previously balanced retrieval relevance and cost inflation. The output is not a user-facing feature; it is an attack recipe showing that external corpus poisoning can raise inference cost substantially.
math: The main mathematical idea is constrained search: choose a document from a huge space of possible word sequences while balancing several scores. One score is retrieval relevance, the degree to which the document looks close to the user's question under the retriever's matching rules. Another score is cost pressure, measured by how much token consumption rises when the model uses the document. A third implicit constraint is answer integrity: the abstract says the attack increases cost without degrading the generated answer, so the document cannot simply sabotage content. Reinforcement learning appears because the attacker receives feedback after trying a document. In plain terms, the writer tries something, observes whether it was retrieved and whether it raised cost, then shifts future writing toward patterns that earned better rewards. Group relative policy optimization means candidates are not judged only in isolation; they are compared against a group so the agent can learn which variations did better than nearby alternatives. The memory component adds a simple but powerful statistical idea: past winners are evidence. Keeping historically best adversarial documents gives the search a reusable set of examples, reducing waste and helping the agent explore around already successful designs. The tradeoff is relevance versus resource exhaustion versus stealth.
dots: This paper sits at the intersection of several recurring conference problems. In retrieval work, many papers ask how to choose a small useful set of documents from a huge collection. Here that same selection machinery becomes the attack surface: if relevance scoring can be persuaded to select poisoned material, retrieval becomes a cost amplifier. In LLM security, the paper shifts attention from making a model say the wrong thing to making it spend too much. That connects it to privacy and security papers where harm can happen through a side channel, meaning an indirect signal such as cost, timing, or resource use rather than the visible answer alone. It also connects to reinforcement learning papers because the attacker is learning a policy for document creation through repeated feedback. Neighboring RAG papers try to prune evidence, manage conflicts, or improve document quality; this paper explains why those controls also matter defensively, because bad retrieved evidence can waste compute even when the answer still looks acceptable.
ww: The attack works, intuitively, because RAG systems trust retrieved text enough to spend expensive model computation on it. A plain language model call has one main input: the prompt. A RAG call has a wider supply chain. The system searches outside sources, chooses documents, combines them with the question, and asks the model to synthesize an answer. Each extra stage creates a place where an attacker can shape what the model has to read. If the poisoned document is relevant enough, the retriever treats it as useful rather than suspicious. If the document is written to encourage longer reasoning or more expansive synthesis, the model may spend more tokens processing and answering. Automated agents improve over hand-written attacks because they can repeatedly test document variants against the two-part goal: get retrieved and raise cost. Memory helps because successful adversarial documents are not random accidents; they contain patterns that can guide later drafts. The abstract's reported results, up to 13.12 times token consumption with more than 90 percent success across three datasets, support the claim that this combination can be potent.
po: The payoff is a clearer threat model for RAG services. Instead of assuming an attacker can control the user's prompt, the paper shows a route through external knowledge poisoning, which is closer to how web-scale retrieval systems can be exposed. It gives the attack a concrete form, RA-ICA, and an implementation path, CREEP with MA-GRPO-trained agents. The reported experiments say the attack can raise token consumption by as much as 13.12 times, succeed more than 90 percent of the time, and preserve the integrity of the generated answer. That matters because a service could suffer higher operating costs without seeing obvious answer corruption.
limits: The abstract does not prove that every RAG deployment is equally vulnerable. The attack assumes the adversary can inject documents into a corpus the system may retrieve from, and that the retriever can be made to select those documents. It also assumes token consumption is a meaningful cost lever for the target service. The result is reported across three real-world datasets, but the abstract does not specify which retrievers, filtering defenses, corpus controls, or deployment policies were tested. Preserving answer integrity is important, yet the abstract does not show how users or automated monitors judged that integrity. Stronger source vetting, document-quality scoring, retrieval pruning, or cost caps could change the attack's effect.
